pos: v. (third person singular present of do; the Authorized Version's form for does, and the hinge of the Bible's tests of a true profession)
etymology: The old English third-person singular ending -eth on the verb do, from Anglo-Saxon deth. The -eth form was already retreating before -es when the Authorized Version was made in 1611; the translators kept it, and it survives in English almost solely because they did.
biblical_def: Doeth is not a curiosity of old spelling but one of the most load-bearing words in the Authorized Version, because Scripture repeatedly tests a man by what he doeth rather than by what he professes. David's indictment of the whole race turns on it: “there is none that doeth good” (Psa 14:1), which Paul takes up in Romans 3 as the proof that no man is justified by works. The Lord Jesus divides His hearers by it: “whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock” (Mat 7:24) — hearing is common to both builders; doing is what the storm exposes. John uses it as the mark of the regenerate: “he that doeth righteousness is righteous, even as he is righteous” (1Jn 3:7), and “he that doeth truth cometh to the light” (Joh 3:21). The doing never earns the standing; it demonstrates it. That is the whole Reformed reading of the epistle of James, and the little word doeth is where the New Testament puts the weight.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives doeth as the third person singular of the verb do, an older form of does, and notes that it is retained in the Scriptures and in solemn style.
webster_full: DOETH, v. The third person singular of the present tense of do; an older form of does.
Note. Doth and doeth are both retained in the common version of the Scriptures, and in solemn discourse.
DO, v.t. To perform; to execute; to carry into effect; to exert labor or power for bringing any thing to the state desired.
2. To practice; to perform; as, to do good or evil.
scriptures: To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. They are corrupt, they have done abominable works, there is none that doeth good.
Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:
Little children, let no man deceive you: he that doeth righteousness is righteous, even as he is righteous.
But he that doeth truth cometh to the light, that his deeds may be made manifest, that they are wrought in God.
corruption_summary: The archaic form is treated as the only thing worth noticing, so that modernising the word quietly modernises the demand — a doer of the word becomes a person on a spiritual path.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest handling of doeth is to dismiss it as quaint and move on, which conceals how sharp the underlying claim is. Scripture does not ask whether a man agrees, resonates, or is on a journey; it asks what he doeth. Mat 7:24 stages the whole question: both men hear the same sermon and both build a house, and the sole recorded difference is doing. Where the register softens, the test softens with it, and a religion of assent quietly replaces a religion of obedience.

The opposite error is to seize on doeth as though it taught justification by works. It does not, and 1Jn 3:7 says why: the man who doeth righteousness is righteous — the doing reveals a nature already given, as fruit reveals a tree. The Reformed order is fixed: regeneration produces faith, faith receives Christ's imputed righteousness, and that righteousness produces doing. Remove the doing altogether and you have not protected grace; you have removed the evidence Scripture itself appeals to.
roots_summary: English -eth, the Anglo-Saxon third-person singular ending; rendering Hebrew imperfect and participial forms of asah (H6213), to do or make, and Greek present participles of poieo (G4160), to do.
roots_lines: Anglo-Saxon -eth — the third-person singular present ending, standard in southern English until the sixteenth century and preserved by the 1611 translators.
Hebrew asah (H6213) — to do, make, accomplish; the participle oseh underlies “none that doeth good” (Psa 14:1).
Greek poieo (G4160) — to do, make, practise; the present participle in 1Jn 3:7 denotes settled practice, not a single act.
Greek ho poion ten aletheian — “he that doeth truth” (Joh 3:21); truth in John is something done as well as believed.
Jas 1:22 — “be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only”; the noun poietes from the same root.
usage: “There is none that doeth good” — the universal indictment Paul cites in Rom 3:12.
“Heareth… and doeth them” — hearing is common to both builders; doing is what the storm tests.
“He that doeth righteousness is righteous” — the doing reveals the nature, it does not create it.

pos: v. (second person singular present of do; the Authorized Version's thou dost, the form of direct personal address)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon dest, the second-person singular of don, to do; contracted in Middle English to dost. It belongs with thou, and it disappeared from English when thou did.
biblical_def: Dost is the form a speaker uses when he addresses one person, directly, to his face. That is its whole value, and it is a value modern English has lost: you now serves for one man and for a thousand, so English Bibles can no longer show at a glance whether God is addressing a nation or a soul. The Authorized Version can. When the angel at Peniel answers Jacob — “Wherefore is it that thou dost ask after my name?” (Gen 32:29) — the singular marks a man alone in the dark with God. When David calls after Saul, “after whom dost thou pursue? after a dead dog, after a flea” (1Sa 24:14), the singular presses the king's conscience personally. When Rabshakeh taunts Hezekiah, “on whom dost thou trust, that thou rebellest against me?” (2Ki 18:20), the whole siege narrows to one king's object of trust. And the Law uses it to make charity personal: “when thou dost lend thy brother any thing, thou shalt not go into his house to fetch his pledge” (Deu 24:10) — the creditor, singular, is forbidden to invade a man's home to seize his own security.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives dost as the second person singular of the present tense of do, used with thou, and notes that it is now confined to the Scriptures and to solemn or poetic style.
webster_full: DOST, v. The second person singular of the present tense of do; as, thou dost.
Note. It is now used only in the solemn style, and in the common version of the Scriptures.
THOU, pron. The second person singular, used in addressing one person only; in familiar language now generally supplied by you.
Note. The distinction between thou and you, singular and plural, is preserved throughout the Scriptures, and is often material to the sense.
scriptures: And Jacob asked him, and said, Tell me, I pray thee, thy name. And he said, Wherefore is it that thou dost ask after my name? And he blessed him there.
After whom is the king of Israel come out? after whom dost thou pursue? after a dead dog, after a flea.
Thou sayest, (but they are but vain words,) I have counsel and strength for the war. Now on whom dost thou trust, that thou rebellest against me?
When thou dost lend thy brother any thing, thou shalt not go into his house to fetch his pledge.
corruption_summary: Thou is heard as lofty and formal, when it is in fact the intimate singular — so the very forms that make Scripture personal are mistaken for the ones that make it remote.
corruption_paragraphs: Almost every modern reader has the sense of thou exactly backwards. In the English of 1611 thou was the familiar singular a man used with his wife, his child, or his God, while you was the plural and the formal address to a superior. Four centuries of disuse have made thou sound like a stained-glass honorific, and so the Authorized Version acquires a reputation for coldness on the strength of the words that are actually its warmest. When the risen Lord asks Peter “lovest thou me?”, the form is the one a man uses to a friend.

There is a real cost in the loss, and it is not aesthetic. Because modern English cannot distinguish singular from plural, whole passages become ambiguous: the reader cannot tell whether a promise is made to a church or to him, whether a warning falls on a nation or on a man. The Authorized Version marks every one of these, and the thou/dost forms are how. Preachers who work from it should say so plainly rather than apologise for it — the archaism carries information the modern versions have to supply with a footnote.
roots_summary: Anglo-Saxon dest, second person singular of don; the whole thou/thee/thy/-est paradigm renders the Hebrew and Greek second-person singular, distinct in both languages from the plural.
roots_lines: Anglo-Saxon dest — thou doest; contracted to dost in Middle English.
Thou (subject), thee (object), thy/thine (possessive) — all singular; ye, you, your are the plurals throughout the Authorized Version.
The -est ending (dost, hast, art, wilt, canst, shalt) marks the second person singular verb.
Hebrew distinguishes attah (thou, m.s.) from attem (ye, m.pl.) in every verb form; the KJV reproduces it exactly.
Greek distinguishes su (thou) from humeis (ye); Luk 22:31-32 turns on it — Satan desired to have you (plural, the apostles), but I have prayed for thee (singular, Peter).
usage: “Wherefore is it that thou dost ask after my name?” — one man alone with God at Peniel.
“On whom dost thou trust?” — a siege narrowed to one king's object of trust.
“When thou dost lend thy brother” — the Law addressing the creditor personally, not the market generally.

pos: v. (second person singular of can; thou canst — the Authorized Version's word for the limit and the reach of a single person's power)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon canst, second person singular of cunnan, to know how, to be able. The root sense is to know, which is why can, cunning, and ken are cousins: the oldest English idea of ability is knowledge, not force.
biblical_def: Canst is the word by which Scripture measures a man against God, and it nearly always returns the same answer. To Moses on the mount: “Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live” (Exo 33:20) — the refusal is mercy, since the sight would kill the man who asked for it. To Job out of the whirlwind of Zophar's challenge: “Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection?” (Job 11:7) — the classic text for the incomprehensibility of God, which does not mean God is unknowable but that He is not exhaustible by the creature's searching. Against this background the leper's use of the word is startling, because he turns it toward Christ: “If thou wilt, thou canst make me clean” (Mar 1:40). The man concedes everything about the will and concedes nothing about the power. That is the shape of true faith — certain of Christ's ability, submissive about His purpose — and the Lord answers both halves at once: “I will; be thou clean.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives canst as the second person singular of can, and defines can as to be able, to have sufficient strength or power, from a root signifying to know.
webster_full: CANST, v. The second person singular of can; as, thou canst.
CAN, v.i. To be able; to have sufficient strength or physical power.
2. To have sufficient means or instruments. A man can build a house, if he has the means.
3. To have adequate moral power. A man can indulge in pleasure, or he can refrain.
Note. The primary sense is to know, as in the Saxon cunnan; whence cunning, and ken.
scriptures: And he said, Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live.
Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection?
And there came a leper to him, beseeching him, and kneeling down to him, and saying unto him, If thou wilt, thou canst make me clean.
To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. They are corrupt, they have done abominable works, there is none that doeth good.
corruption_summary: Job 11:7 is quoted to license agnosticism — if God cannot be found out by searching, then no one may claim to know Him — which is the opposite of what the incomprehensibility of God has ever meant.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is a favourite of every framework that wants theology to end in a shrug, from liberal Protestantism's reduction of doctrine to religious feeling to the popular claim that all confident theology is arrogance. But the Reformed doctrine of incomprehensibility says something precise and something hopeful: God cannot be known exhaustively by the creature, and He can be known truly because He has revealed Himself. Deu 29:29 sets the two halves side by side — the secret things belong unto the LORD, but the things revealed belong unto us and to our children. A God who could be found out by searching would be an idol; a God who could not be known at all would leave Scripture pointless.

Exo 33:20 shows the same structure. Moses is refused the face and granted the back parts and the proclaimed name (Exo 34:6-7) — that is, denied the vision that would consume him and given the self-disclosure he can bear. The limit is not divine reticence but divine kindness. And Mar 1:40 shows what a man is to do with the limit: not speculate about it, but come to Christ, in whom “dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (Col 2:9), and say thou canst.
roots_summary: Anglo-Saxon cunnan, to know how, to be able — the source of can, canst, cunning, and ken; rendering Hebrew yakol (H3201), to be able, and Greek dunamai (G1410), to have power.
roots_lines: Anglo-Saxon cunnan — to know how; the second person singular canst. English ability begins as knowledge.
Hebrew yakol (H3201) — to be able, to prevail; the verb behind “thou canst not see my face”.
Hebrew matsa (H4672) — to find, find out; Job 11:7 asks whether the creature can find out God by searching.
Greek dunamai (G1410) — to be able, to have power; the leper's dunasai, “thou canst” (Mar 1:40), from which English gets dynamic.
Greek thelo (G2309) — to will; the leper distinguishes will from power, and Christ answers both: thelo, katharistheti.
usage: “Thou canst not see my face” — a refusal that is mercy to the man who asked.
“Canst thou by searching find out God?” — incomprehensible, not unknowable.
“If thou wilt, thou canst make me clean” — certain of the power, submissive about the purpose.

pos: pron. (whoever; the Authorized Version's shorter form of whosoever, introducing a universal statute or a universal promise)
etymology: A contraction of whosoever — Middle English who so, that is, who ever it may be. The Authorized Version uses both forms, whoso chiefly in the Law, the Psalms, and Proverbs, whosoever more often in the Gospels.
biblical_def: Whoso opens a sentence that admits of no exceptions, and Scripture uses it for both edges of the sword. It states universal law: “Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man” (Gen 9:6) — the Noahic charter of capital justice, grounded not in deterrence but in the image of God borne by the victim. It states universal promise: “Whoso offereth praise glorifieth me” (Psa 50:23), and “Whoso is wise, and will observe these things, even they shall understand the lovingkindness of the LORD” (Psa 107:43) — the closing line of the great psalm of the redeemed, which makes understanding a matter of attention rather than of cleverness. And it states universal test: “whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?” (1Jn 3:17). In each case the word refuses the reader an exemption. It is the grammar of a law that binds every man and a mercy that excludes no comer.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives whoso as a compound relative pronoun equivalent to whosoever, meaning any person whatever, and notes that it is now chiefly used in the Scriptures and in poetry.
webster_full: WHOSO, pron. Any one; any person whatever; a compound relative, equivalent to whosoever.
Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed. Gen. ix.
WHOSOEVER, pron. Any one without exception; any person whatever.
Note. Whoso is the elder and shorter form, retained in the common version and in poetry.
scriptures: Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.
Whoso is wise, and will observe these things, even they shall understand the lovingkindness of the LORD.
But whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?
Whoso offereth praise glorifieth me: and to him that ordereth his conversation aright will I shew the salvation of God.
corruption_summary: Gen 9:6 is set aside as primitive, and the universal whoso of the gospel promise is narrowed by systems that will not let the offer stand as broad as the word.
corruption_paragraphs: Gen 9:6 is the standing biblical warrant for capital justice, and it is regularly dismissed as an artefact of a harsher age. But the verse supplies its own reason, and the reason is not vengeance: for in the image of God made he man. The gravity of murder is measured by the dignity of the victim, and a society that abolishes the penalty on the grounds of the murderer's dignity has quietly transferred the image of God from the one killed to the one who killed. The magistrate's sword in Rom 13:4 stands in the same line.

The opposite narrowing happens with the promises. The dictionary holds definite atonement — Christ's work is effectual for the elect and not a mere possibility for all — and precisely because that is settled, the free offer of the gospel may go out as wide as Scripture makes it. Whoso and whosoever are the Bible's own words, and no preacher has warrant to add a qualifier the Holy Ghost did not write. The Reformed tradition has always held both: the secret decree of election belongs to God, and the universal call belongs to the pulpit.
roots_summary: Middle English who so, whoever; rendering Hebrew constructions with mi asher or a bare participle, and Greek hos an / hostis, the indefinite relative.
roots_lines: Middle English who so — “who ever it may be”; the so is the old generalising particle, as in howsoever.
Hebrew participial law-formulas — Gen 9:6 is literally “shedder of the blood of the man”, a participle standing for any and every such man.
Hebrew mi (H4310) — who; with asher it forms the indefinite “whoever” of the statutes.
Greek hos an — whoever, with the subjunctive; the ordinary Greek for an open-ended condition.
Greek hostis (G3748) — whoever, whichever; the form behind many of the Gospels' “whosoever” sayings.
usage: “Whoso sheddeth man's blood” — a statute grounded in the image of God, not in deterrence.
“Whoso is wise, and will observe” — understanding given to attention, not to cleverness.
“Whoso hath this world's good” — the test of a professed love of God is an open hand.

pos: n. and adv. (nothing; hence for nought, without payment or without cause, and to nought, to ruin)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon nawiht — ne (not) plus a (ever) plus wiht (thing, creature): literally not ever a thing. The same word gives us naught and, weakened, not. The wight of old English for a creature is the surviving third piece.
biblical_def: Nought does three jobs in the Authorized Version. For nought means without payment: Laban asks Jacob, “shouldest thou therefore serve me for nought? tell me, what shall thy wages be?” (Gen 29:15) — and the question is honest even though Laban will prove a cheat, because Scripture holds that a labourer is worthy of his hire. For nought also means without cause, and this is the hinge of the book of Job: Satan's challenge is “Doth Job fear God for nought?” (Job 1:9) — the accusation that no creature loves God for Himself, but only for the hedge and the herds. The whole book is God's answer to that single sentence, and Job's worship on the ash-heap is the answer. To nought means to ruin: “The LORD bringeth the counsel of the heathen to nought” (Psa 33:10); and Gamaliel's prudential argument in Acts rests on the same principle — Theudas rose, and his followers “were scattered, and brought to nought” (Act 5:36), so that what is of men will fall of itself and what is of God cannot be overthrown.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines nought as nothing, and notes the phrases to set at nought, to slight or despise, and to come to nought, to be ruined or brought to nothing.
webster_full: NOUGHT, n. Nothing.
Doth Job fear God for nought? Job i.
2. To set at nought, to slight, disregard or despise.
3. To come, or be brought to nought, to be ruined or reduced to nothing.
Note. It is written also naught, from the Saxon nawiht, ne aht, not any thing.
scriptures: Then Satan answered the LORD, and said, Doth Job fear God for nought?
And Laban said unto Jacob, Because thou art my brother, shouldest thou therefore serve me for nought? tell me, what shall thy wages be?
The LORD bringeth the counsel of the heathen to nought: he maketh the devices of the people of none effect.

For before these days rose up Theudas, boasting himself to be somebody; to whom a number of men, about four hundred, joined themselves: who was slain; and all, as many as obeyed him, were scattered, and brought to nought.
corruption_summary: Satan's question in Job 1:9 is answered wrongly by the prosperity gospel, which builds a religion on precisely the motive the accuser alleged.
corruption_paragraphs: “Doth Job fear God for nought?” is the accuser's thesis: that piety is always a transaction, and that no man would worship a God who paid nothing. The prosperity preachers of the modern American church — the seed-faith, name-it-and-claim-it, sow-into-this-ministry apparatus — have unwittingly agreed with him and made his thesis their doctrine. Where God is preached as the reliable dispenser of health and money in return for faith and giving, worship is a transaction, and Satan's question has been answered in his favour by the pulpit.

Job answers it the other way, and answers it stripped: “the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD” (Job 1:21). That is worship for nought — without payment, without cause outside God Himself — and it is the only kind that proves anything. Psa 33:10 supplies the comfort underneath it. The counsel of the heathen comes to nought; the devices of the people are made of none effect; and the man who serves God for nothing has hitched himself to the one purpose in the universe that cannot be brought to nought.
roots_summary: Anglo-Saxon nawiht, not-ever-a-thing; rendering Hebrew chinnam (H2600), gratis or without cause, and Greek phrases with ouden, nothing.
roots_lines: Anglo-Saxon nawiht — ne + a + wiht, not ever a thing; also the source of naught and, worn down, of not.
Hebrew chinnam (H2600) — freely, gratis, without cause; from chen, favour. It is the word in Job 1:9, and also in “they hated me without a cause” (Psa 69:4; Joh 15:25).
Hebrew parar (H6565) — to break, frustrate; “bringeth the counsel of the heathen to nought” (Psa 33:10).
Greek oudeis / ouden (G3762) — no one, nothing; the base of the New Testament's “come to nought”.
Greek exoutheneo (G1848) — to set at nought, treat as nothing; used of Herod's men mocking Christ (Luk 23:11).
usage: “Serve me for nought” — without wages; the labourer is worthy of his hire.
“Doth Job fear God for nought?” — the accuser's thesis that all piety is a transaction.
“Bringeth the counsel of the heathen to nought” — every device against God is already frustrated.

pos: adv. (at or to a distance; almost always in the phrase afar off, marking the distance sin keeps and faith crosses)
etymology: From a- (on, at) plus far, Anglo-Saxon feorr. The a- is the same locative prefix as in aboard, abroad, ashore — it means on or in, not away.
biblical_def: Afar off is one of the Authorized Version's most theologically loaded phrases, because distance in Scripture is rarely only geography. At Sinai it is the distance of a holy God from a sinful people: “the people stood afar off, and Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was” (Exo 20:21) — and the whole apparatus of mediation exists because of that gap. In Genesis it is the distance of faith's obedience: “on the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes, and saw the place afar off” (Gen 22:4), three days of walking toward the hardest command ever given a father. In Hebrews it is the distance of promise: the patriarchs “died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them” (Heb 11:13) — faith embracing what it will not live to hold. And in the parable it is the distance of true repentance: “the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner” (Luk 18:13). The man who knows he stands afar off is the man who goes home justified.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines afar as at a distance in place, and notes that it is chiefly used with off, and in Scripture of remoteness in time or in condition as well as in place.
webster_full: AFAR, adv. At a distance in place; to or from a distance; used with from preceding, or off following.
They stood afar off. Ex. xx.
2. In Scripture, it denotes remoteness of time or of condition, as well as of place.
Note. From a and far; the prefix a signifying on or at.
scriptures: And the people stood afar off, and Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was.
Then on the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes, and saw the place afar off.
And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner.

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
corruption_summary: The distance at Sinai is read as evidence of a harsh Old Testament God whom the New Testament later softens — a division of the Testaments that Scripture nowhere makes.
corruption_paragraphs: Marcion made the split in the second century and it has never stopped resurfacing: the God of thunder and distance in Exodus, the God of nearness and welcome in the Gospels. But the same God set the bounds at Sinai and tore the veil at Calvary, and the second act is unintelligible without the first. The people stand afar off because they are sinners and He is holy; if that distance is not real, the rending of the veil is theatre. Eph 2:13 keeps both: “ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ” — made nigh, at a price, from a real distance.

Luk 18:13 shows how the distance is to be handled by the man who feels it. The publican does not argue himself closer or claim a standing he lacks; he stands afar off, will not lift his eyes, and asks for mercy on the ground of atonement — the verb is the one used of the mercy seat. And he, not the Pharisee at the front, goes down to his house justified. The gospel does not deny the distance; it crosses it, and it will not be crossed by the man who pretends it was never there.
roots_summary: English a- plus far; rendering Hebrew rachoq (H7350), distant, from rachaq, to be far, and Greek makrothen (G3113), from afar.
roots_lines: Hebrew rachoq (H7350) — far, distant; the word of Exo 20:21 and of Gen 22:4.
Hebrew rachaq (H7368) — to be or become far; used of removing transgressions “as far as the east is from the west” (Psa 103:12).
Greek makrothen (G3113) — from a distance; the publican's position (Luk 18:13) and the women at the cross (Mat 27:55).
Greek porrothen (G4207) — from afar; the patriarchs seeing the promises (Heb 11:13) and the ten lepers standing off (Luk 17:12).
Eph 2:13, 17 — makran, afar off, of the Gentiles; “made nigh by the blood of Christ”, the distance abolished at a price.
usage: “The people stood afar off” — the real distance that mediation exists to cross.
“Saw the place afar off” — three days' walk toward the hardest command.
“Standing afar off” — the publican who owns the distance goes home justified.

pos: adv. (always, perpetually; in the Authorized Version chiefly for evermore, the settled unending state of a thing God has established)
etymology: From ever (Anglo-Saxon aefre) plus more — an intensified ever, as one might say ever and further. English built the compound to say more than ever alone could.
biblical_def: Evermore is not a mere synonym for always; in the Authorized Version it usually attaches to something God has settled and will not revisit. It fixes the throne: “I will settle him in mine house and in my kingdom for ever: and his throne shall be established for evermore” (1Ch 17:14) — the Davidic covenant, whose terms reach past Solomon to the Son of David whose kingdom has no end. It fixes the believer's portion: “in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore” (Psa 16:11) — a verse Peter preaches at Pentecost as a prophecy of the resurrection, so that the pleasures for evermore are secured by an empty tomb and not by an optimistic temperament. And Paul turns it into a command in the shortest verse of his letters: “Rejoice evermore” (1Th 5:16), which is only issuable as a command because the ground of the joy is outside the circumstances. The crowd at Capernaum uses it too, and wrongly: “Lord, evermore give us this bread” (Joh 6:34) — asking for a perpetual supply of loaves from the One who was offering them Himself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines evermore as always, eternally, at all times, and notes the phrase for evermore as denoting an unending continuance.
webster_full: EVERMORE, adv. Always; eternally; at all times.
He shall be blessed for evermore. Ps. xxxvii.
2. Continually; without intermission.
Note. Compounded of ever and more, an intensive form of ever.
scriptures: Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.
But I will settle him in mine house and in my kingdom for ever: and his throne shall be established for evermore.
Then said they unto him, Lord, evermore give us this bread.
corruption_summary: The unending state is emptied at both ends — annihilationism ends the punishment, and universalism ends the distinction — so that for evermore is left describing nothing in particular.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture uses the same vocabulary of unending duration for the blessedness of the redeemed and the punishment of the unredeemed, and it uses it in the same sentence at Mat 25:46: “these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal”. Annihilationism, now common among evangelicals who find the doctrine intolerable, must break the parallel and read one everlasting as unending and the other as terminal. Universalism must break it the other way. Both proposals rest on what God's love would supposedly not allow rather than on what God has said, and both leave the believer's evermore resting on the same weakened word.

The doctrine is not cruelty; it is the seriousness of sin against an infinitely worthy God, and the LBCF holds it plainly. It is also what makes Psa 16:11 worth anything. Pleasures for evermore are only a comfort if evermore means what it says, and Peter's use of the psalm at Pentecost (Act 2:25-28) ties the promise to a fact in history — the flesh that did not see corruption. The command of 1Th 5:16 stands on the same ground: rejoice evermore, because the thing you rejoice in has been settled for evermore.
roots_summary: English ever + more; rendering Hebrew olam (H5769), the age or perpetuity, often with ad (H5703), and Greek pantote (G3842), always, or eis tous aionas, unto the ages.
roots_lines: Hebrew olam (H5769) — the hidden or unbounded time; “for ever” and “for evermore” both render it.
Hebrew ad olam — unto perpetuity; the phrase of 1Ch 17:14, of the Davidic throne.
Hebrew netsach (H5331) — enduring, everlasting; “pleasures for evermore” in Psa 16:11.
Greek pantote (G3842) — always, at all times; Paul's command chairete pantote, Rejoice evermore (1Th 5:16).
Greek eis ton aiona — unto the age; the Septuagint and New Testament rendering of olam, and the phrase Christ uses of the Comforter abiding “for ever” (Joh 14:16).
usage: “His throne shall be established for evermore” — the Davidic covenant, settled and not revisited.
“Pleasures for evermore” — secured by resurrection, not by temperament.
“Lord, evermore give us this bread” — asking a perpetual supply of loaves from the Bread Himself.

pos: adv. (with that; with the thing just named — the Authorized Version's compact way of pointing back without repeating)
etymology: From there plus with, one of a large family of English compounds — thereof, thereby, therein, thereto, thereon, therefore — in which there stands for the thing just mentioned. They allowed the translators great precision without pronouns that might attach to the wrong noun.
biblical_def: Therewith means with that thing, and the Authorized Version uses it where a modern version must either repeat the noun or risk ambiguity. In the Law it points to the instrument of atonement: “the priest that maketh atonement therewith shall have it” (Lev 7:7) — the priest who officiates with the trespass offering receives his portion of it, an ordinance Paul invokes when he argues that they which minister about holy things live of the things of the temple. In Judges it points to the unlikeliest weapon in Scripture: Samson “found a new jawbone of an ass, and put forth his hand, and took it, and slew a thousand men therewith” (Jdg 15:15). And in Paul it points to whatever a Christian happens to have: “having food and raiment let us be therewith content” (1Ti 6:8), and “I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content” (Php 4:11). That last is the word's finest use. Contentment in the New Testament is not contentment in general but contentment with that — with the specific, named, often meagre thing in hand.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines therewith as with this, or with that, and notes it as one of the compounds of there used in place of a pronoun with its preposition.
webster_full: THEREWITH, adv. With this or that.
Having food and raiment, let us be therewith content. 1 Tim. vi.
2. Immediately after; upon that.
Note. Of the same class are thereof, thereby, therein, thereto, thereon, whereof, whereby, wherein.
scriptures: Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
And having food and raiment let us be therewith content.
As the sin offering is, so is the trespass offering: there is one law for them: the priest that maketh atonement therewith shall have it.
And he found a new jawbone of an ass, and put forth his hand, and took it, and slew a thousand men therewith.
corruption_summary: Contentment is recast as a feeling to be cultivated by technique — gratitude practices, mindfulness, reframing — when Paul presents it as something learned under the providence of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Php 4:11 is the most quoted verse on the subject and the most consistently mishandled. Paul does not say he possesses a serene disposition; he says “I have learned”, and the next verse names the curriculum: “I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound… both to be full and to be hungry”. The teacher is providence and the lessons are hunger and plenty, taken in order and taken from God's hand. Reduce this to a mental technique and it becomes something a man does to himself; keep it as Paul wrote it and it is something God does to a man, with the strength named in verse 13.

1Ti 6:8 sets the bar embarrassingly low — food and covering — and Paul's point in context is that godliness with contentment is great gain, over against those who suppose gain is godliness. The therapeutic reframing of contentment leaves the appetite intact and merely manages the distress it causes; the apostolic version kills the appetite by relocating the treasure. The little word therewith is the whole difference: content with that, the actual portion, not with an improved feeling about wanting more.
roots_summary: English there + with; standing for Hebrew prepositional suffixes (bo, with it) and Greek constructions with en toutois or the dative, as in autarkes contexts.
roots_lines: English there- compounds — thereof, thereby, therein, therewith: there substitutes for the noun just named, giving precision without repetition.
Hebrew prepositional suffixes — a single letter b- with a pronoun ending says “with it”; English needs two words, and the KJV supplies one.
Greek autarkes (G842) — self-sufficient, content; Paul's word at Php 4:11, borrowed from the Stoics and emptied of its self-reliance.
Greek autarkeia (G841) — contentment, sufficiency; “godliness with contentment is great gain” (1Ti 6:6).
Greek arkeo (G714) — to be enough; “let us be therewith content” (1Ti 6:8) is literally “we shall be sufficed with these”.
usage: “Therewith to be content” — content with that, the actual portion, not with a better feeling.
“Slew a thousand men therewith” — the instrument God is pleased to use is often the one at hand.
“Maketh atonement therewith” — the officiating priest has his portion of the offering.

pos: adv. (from, away; surviving in English only in the pair to and fro, which the Authorized Version uses for restless, purposeless motion)
etymology: From Old Norse fra, from — a Scandinavian import that once stood alongside the native from and has now shrunk to a single fixed phrase. Fro is the going away; to is the coming back; together they name motion without arrival.
biblical_def: To and fro in Scripture almost always describes movement that gets nowhere, and the Authorized Version uses it with striking consistency. The raven from the ark “went forth to and fro, until the waters were dried up from off the earth” (Gen 8:7) — an unclean bird that finds carrion enough and never returns, against the dove that finds no rest and comes back. Satan gives the phrase its most famous use twice: asked whence he comes, he answers, “From going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it” (Job 1:7) — a restless patrol, a prowling without a home, which Peter later renders as a lion walking about seeking whom he may devour. Paul takes the same phrase into the doctrine of the church: believers are to be “no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14) — the drifting of the untaught, which the gift of pastors and teachers exists to end. And Daniel is told that at the time of the end “many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased” (Dan 12:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives fro as from, away, backward, and notes that it is used chiefly in the phrase to and fro, that is, forward and backward, hither and thither.
webster_full: FRO, adv. From; away; backward.
To and fro, backward and forward; hither and thither.
Note. It is now used only in this phrase, and is a contraction of the Gothic and Saxon fram, from.
Note. From going to and fro in the earth. Job i.
scriptures: And the LORD said unto Satan, Whence comest thou? Then Satan answered the LORD, and said, From going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.
And he sent forth a raven, which went forth to and fro, until the waters were dried up from off the earth.
That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;
But thou, O Daniel, shut up the words, and seal the book, even to the time of the end: many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased.
corruption_summary: Job 1:7 is read as though Satan roams at will, and Eph 4:14 as though doctrinal drift were harmless exploration rather than the mark of spiritual infancy.
corruption_paragraphs: The scene in Job 1 is often preached as evidence of a devil with the run of the world, which gets the chapter exactly backwards. Satan comes when summoned, answers when questioned, and can do nothing to Job's goods or body without explicit permission and explicit limits: “behold, all that he hath is in thy power; only upon himself put not forth thine hand” (Job 1:12). The going to and fro is real and it is bounded. Nothing in the book supports the dualism that treats God and Satan as rival powers; the accuser is a creature on a leash, and the leash is held.

Eph 4:14 addresses the modern instinct that treats doctrinal instability as intellectual honesty. Paul calls it childishness — being tossed to and fro, the passive of a small boat in a swell — and he names its cause, the sleight and craftiness of men who lie in wait to deceive. His remedy is not less doctrine but more: the ascended Christ gave pastors and teachers precisely so that the church would stop drifting. A congregation with no settled confession has not achieved openness; it has been left in infancy.
roots_summary: Old Norse fra, from; rendering Hebrew idioms of going out and returning (shut, to rove) and Greek kludonizomai (G2831), to be tossed by waves.
roots_lines: Old Norse fra — from; a Danelaw borrowing that survives only in to and fro.
Hebrew shut (H7751) — to rove, go to and fro; Satan's word in Job 1:7 and 2:2, and the LORD's eyes running to and fro in 2Ch 16:9.
Hebrew halak (H1980) — to walk, go; “walking up and down in it”, paired with shut for restless patrol.
Greek kludonizomai (G2831) — to be tossed by the surge; Eph 4:14, of the doctrinally unsettled.
Greek peripatei in 1Pe 5:8 — the adversary “walketh about, seeking whom he may devour”, the New Testament echo of Job 1:7.
usage: “Going to and fro in the earth” — restless patrol, and bounded at every step.
“Tossed to and fro… with every wind of doctrine” — drift is infancy, not honesty.
“Went forth to and fro” — the raven that never came back to the ark.

pos: adv. (entirely, completely, without reserve; the Authorized Version's word for an undivided offering and an undivided man)
etymology: From whole (Anglo-Saxon hal, sound, entire — the same root as hale, heal, and holy) plus -ly. The English words for entire, healthy, and holy grow from one stock, which is itself a small sermon: to be holy is to be whole, undivided, unbroken toward God.
biblical_def: Wholly marks the difference between a portion and the whole, and Scripture applies it in three registers. In sacrifice: the priest's meat offering is not shared as others are — “every meat offering for the priest shall be wholly burnt: it shall not be eaten” (Lev 6:23). The man who eats of other men's offerings keeps nothing of his own; what he brings goes entirely up in smoke. In discipleship: of the twelve spies only two survive the verdict, and the reason given is this word — “Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenezite, and Joshua the son of Nun: for they have wholly followed the LORD” (Num 32:12). Ten followed partly; two followed wholly; the difference was forty years and a generation of graves. In sanctification: “the very God of peace sanctify you wholly; and I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1Th 5:23) — a prayer for the entire man, and a prayer addressed to God, because no part of it is within the believer's power to accomplish. Paul then presses the same word onto a young minister: “give thyself wholly to them” (1Ti 4:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wholly as entirely, completely, perfectly — and also as totally, in all the parts or kinds, noting its use for an undivided devotion.
webster_full: WHOLLY, adv. Entirely; completely; perfectly.
He is wholly employed in his own affairs.
2. Totally; in all the parts or kinds.
They employed themselves wholly in domestic affairs.
Note. From whole, Saxon hal, sound, entire; whence also heal, health, and holy.
scriptures: Save Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenezite, and Joshua the son of Nun: for they have wholly followed the LORD.
And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly; and I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Meditate upon these things; give thyself wholly to them; that thy profiting may appear to all.
For every meat offering for the priest shall be wholly burnt: it shall not be eaten.
corruption_summary: 1Th 5:23 is pressed into the doctrine of entire sanctification — a second work of grace ending the believer's struggle with sin in this life — which the verse's own grammar and horizon forbid.
corruption_paragraphs: The Wesleyan-holiness reading, carried into much of the modern charismatic movement, takes sanctify you wholly as the promise of a crisis experience after which indwelling sin is eradicated. Paul's sentence points elsewhere. It is a prayer, not a claim; its subject is the very God of peace, not the believer's consecration; and its horizon is explicit — “preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ”. The wholeness prayed for is completed at His appearing, which is exactly where 1Jn 3:2 puts it. Romans 7 and Gal 5:17 describe the interim, and the LBCF describes it after them: the war remains, and the regenerate part overcomes.

What the word does demand now is undividedness of aim, and Num 32:12 is the standing example. Ten spies did not apostatise; they simply followed partly, hedging the report with giants. Caleb and Joshua followed wholly, and Scripture records the phrase about them five separate times. The call is not to sinless perfection but to an undivided allegiance — which is why 1Ti 4:15 can command it of a young pastor as a matter of daily practice: meditate, give thyself wholly, and let the profiting appear.
roots_summary: Anglo-Saxon hal, whole, sound — the root also of heal and holy; rendering Hebrew male (H4390), to fill or fulfil, in “wholly followed”, and Greek holoteles (G3651), complete to the end.
roots_lines: Anglo-Saxon hal — sound, entire; the shared root of whole, hale, heal, health, and holy.
Hebrew male achare YHWH — literally “filled up after the LORD”; the KJV's “wholly followed the LORD” (Num 32:12; Deu 1:36; Josh 14:8-9, 14).
Hebrew kalil (H3632) — entire, whole burnt; the technical term for an offering wholly consumed (Lev 6:22-23).
Greek holoteles (G3651) — wholly, complete through to the end; used once, at 1Th 5:23.
Greek en toutois isthi — literally “be in these things”, the KJV's “give thyself wholly to them” (1Ti 4:15); the man is to live inside his calling.
usage: “They have wholly followed the LORD” — two men out of twelve, and the phrase repeated of them ever after.
“Sanctify you wholly” — a prayer to God with its horizon at Christ's coming.
“Wholly burnt” — the priest's own offering, of which he keeps nothing.
